promise: After this you can explain what sharding is, how a shard key routes a query, and what you give up when data is split.

terms.definition: A piece of a larger data set, held and served separately from the others.
The field whose value decides which partition a row belongs to.
The component that sends each query to the shard or shards that hold its data.

before.note: Read Replication and Consistent Hashing first: sharding splits data across machines and reuses the ring to place it, while each shard is usually replicated. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: Replication makes copies of the same data, but one machine can only hold and write so much. MongoDB's page defines sharding as a method for distributing data across multiple machines, used when the data set or write rate outgrows one. Each shard holds a subset of the sharded data [[mongodb-sharding]].

The point is horizontal scale for both storage and writes. Reads could already be spread across replicas, but every write still went to one primary. MongoDB lists advantages of sharding for reads and writes, with the workload distributed across the shards, and for storage capacity [[mongodb-sharding]].

Sharding is not the same as partitioning within one server, though they share ideas. PostgreSQL's page describes partitioning a table into pieces on one database server, with built-in range, list and hash forms, and gives a rule of thumb that a table should exceed the server's physical memory before partitioning is worth it [[pg-partitioning]]. Sharding takes partitions across many machines, so the scale and failure story are different.

terms.definition: One partition of a data set, held on its own machine or replica set.
Splitting a table into pieces; sharding spreads those pieces across machines.
The field whose value decides which shard a row belongs to.
Adding machines to handle more data and writes, rather than enlarging one machine.
How many writes per second the system can accept; sharding raises it by spreading writes.

stages.name: How it works
body: Everything turns on the shard key and how its values map to shards. MongoDB says it uses the shard key to distribute a collection's documents across shards, and supports two strategies. Hashed sharding computes a hash of the shard key value and assigns each chunk a range of hashed values. Ranged sharding divides data into ranges of shard key values, so keys whose values are close are more likely to live together [[mongodb-sharding]].

Hash-based placement is where consistent hashing returns. Dynamo describes treating the output of a hash function as a ring, with each node at a position on it, so a key's hash decides which node owns it and adding or removing a node affects only its neighbours [[dynamo]]. The ring you learned earlier is one mechanism for hash placement; Redis Cluster's fixed hash slots are another.

A router sits between clients and shards. MongoDB's page says a mongos acts as a query router between client applications and the sharded cluster, while config servers store the cluster's metadata [[mongodb-sharding]]. When a query names the shard key, the router can send it to the shard that holds the data; when it does not, it has to ask every shard and merge the results, which is much more expensive. MongoDB notes that with hashed sharding, range queries on the shard key are less likely to target a single shard and cause more cluster-wide broadcast operations [[mongodb-sharding]].

Picking the shard key is the single most important decision. A good key spreads both data and traffic evenly and lets common queries target one shard. A poor key sends most traffic to one shard, a hot shard, or forces most queries to scatter to all shards.

terms.definition: Assigning contiguous key ranges to shards; good for range scans, risky for even spread.
Hashing the key before placing it, which spreads neighbours and writes evenly.
A query that names the shard key, so the router hits only one shard.
A query without the shard key, which must ask every shard and merge the results.
A shard taking far more than its share of traffic because of a poor shard key.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Shards drift out of balance as data grows unevenly, so systems rebalance by moving chunks of data between shards. MongoDB partitions sharded data into chunks, each with a range of shard key values, and says a balancer runs in the background to migrate ranges across the shards and keep the data evenly distributed [[mongodb-sharding]].

Some operations get hard once data is split. A query that joins or aggregates across shards must gather partial results from each and combine them. A transaction that touches more than one shard needs coordination to stay atomic, which is slower and more complex than a single-shard transaction. The cheapest designs keep related data on the same shard so these cross-shard operations are rare. This is general reasoning; the cited pages do not cover cross-shard transactions.

Sharding and replication combine rather than compete. MongoDB says each shard must be deployed as a replica set, so a shard is really a small replicated cluster [[mongodb-sharding]]. DynamoDB describes storing data in partitions that are automatically replicated across multiple Availability Zones, so the data is split and each piece survives a machine loss [[dynamo-partitions]].

terms.definition: A contiguous group of documents MongoDB moves as a unit when rebalancing.
Moving data between shards to keep their sizes and load even.
A query whose data spans shards, needing results gathered and combined.
A transaction touching more than one shard, needing coordination to stay atomic.
A single shard kept on several replicas, so it survives a machine failure.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The deepest trade-off is that sharding adds permanent complexity to buy scale. Routing, rebalancing, cross-shard queries and multi-shard transactions all become harder, so the usual advice is to shard only when a single replicated database can no longer cope, not before. MongoDB frames sharding as a response to the data and write limits of a single machine [[mongodb-sharding]].

The shard key is costly to change. Once data is spread by a key and queries are written around it, changing it means redistributing the data. MongoDB 5.0 and later can reshard a collection by changing its shard key, but its page still tells you to choose the key carefully [[mongodb-sharding]]. A key that spreads load today but concentrates tomorrow's hot data, like a monotonically increasing timestamp sending all new writes to one shard, is a classic trap. Hashed sharding avoids that at the cost of range scans, as MongoDB's note on range queries shows [[mongodb-sharding]].

Range versus hash is the recurring practical choice. Ranged sharding keeps neighbours together, so range scans hit few shards, but risks hot shards at the end of the range. Hashed sharding spreads writes evenly but makes range scans cluster-wide broadcasts [[mongodb-sharding]]. PostgreSQL's partitioning page offers the same menu inside one server, range, list and hash, and the right answer follows your dominant query pattern [[pg-partitioning]].

terms.definition: The ongoing cost of running a sharded system: routing, rebalancing and cross-shard work.
A key that always increases, like a timestamp, which can send all new writes to one shard.
Changing the shard key or shard count, which forces redistributing the data.
The mix of reads and writes your app does, which should drive the shard key and strategy.

misconceptions.truth: They combine: MongoDB says each shard must be deployed as a replica set, and DynamoDB replicates each partition across Availability Zones [[mongodb-sharding]] [[dynamo-partitions]].

misconceptions.myth: Any shard key works as long as it is unique.
misconceptions.truth: A poor key, like an increasing timestamp, concentrates traffic on one shard; the key must spread load and suit queries. MongoDB says it uses the shard key to distribute documents across shards [[mongodb-sharding]].
MongoDB notes that range queries on a hashed shard key are less likely to target a single shard, resulting in more cluster-wide broadcast operations [[mongodb-sharding]].

misconceptions.myth: You can change the shard key later if you get it wrong.
misconceptions.truth: Changing it means redistributing the data. MongoDB 5.0 and later can reshard a collection by changing its shard key, but its page says to choose carefully, so plan the key around your main queries [[mongodb-sharding]].
